items.title: 18.7.2 Ligand Exchange Reactions of Cobalt(II) Complexes

source_refs.note: Topic 18.7.2 (PDF 28-29); Figures 18.9 and 18.10 are replaced by an original diagram.

blocks.text: Cobalt(II) salts also form complex ions in water: Co2+(aq) means [Co(H2O)6]2+, which gives cobalt(II) sulphate solution its pink colour.

blocks.caption: Ligand exchange reactions of cobalt(II)
rows: pink solution gives a blue precipitate, which may turn pink on standing
a soluble hexaamminecobalt(II) ion; yellow solution
water ligands exchanged directly by ammonia

blocks.alt: Top row: pink [Co(H2O)6]2+ solution; adding NaOH gives a blue precipitate of [Co(H2O)4(OH)2], which may turn pink on standing; excess NH3 gives a yellow (straw) solution of [Co(NH3)6]2+. Bottom row: conc. HCl turns pink octahedral [Co(H2O)6]2+ into blue tetrahedral [CoCl4]2-; water gives it back.
blocks.caption: Ligand exchange and colour changes of cobalt(II) complexes (original diagram after Figures 18.9 and 18.10).
blocks.long_description: The cobalt(II) ion behaves in a similar way. Hydroxide ions give a blue precipitate of cobalt(II) hydroxide; excess ammonia replaces the water and hydroxide ligands to give the soluble hexaamminecobalt(II) ion, which is yellow. Concentrated hydrochloric acid gives the blue tetrahedral tetrachlorocobaltate(II) ion. The change from pink to blue also comes with a change of shape and coordination number, from octahedral (6) to tetrahedral (4).

blocks.text: Aqueous cobalt(II) ions usually form tetrahedral complexes with monodentate anionic ligands such as Cl-, OH- and SCN-.
